candidates.title: Robustness of Deterministic Runtime Validators to Model/State Mismatch in LLM-driven NetOps
candidates.research_question: How does increasing model/state mismatch and sensing error affect the false-acceptance and false-rejection rates of deterministic runtime validators (deterministic twins/shields) applied to LLM-generated network configuration changes for reachability and ACL tasks?
hypotheses: Under matched-model/state conditions, a deterministic runtime validator will reduce unsafe-acceptance (false-acceptance) of LLM-generated configs by ≥80% relative to no validator.

Introducing bounded state mismatch and sensing noise will increase the validator's false-rejection rate and will degrade unsafe-acceptance reduction such that beyond a measurable mismatch threshold the validator's net operational utility (accepted-correct/total-accepted) falls below the no-validator baseline.
candidates.proposed_design: Controlled, preregistered experiment using public synthetic and vendor-agnostic topologies: (1) construct a task set of intent-to-configuration problems (reachability, ACL-compliance, loop/blackhole avoidance) using public config fragments; (2) generate candidate configs with one LLM family under fixed prompts; (3) apply a deterministic validator (reachability/ACL oracle implemented via simulator-based symbolic checks) under multiple mismatch conditions: matched state, small sensing perturbation, medium perturbation, large perturbation (perturbations change link status, device state, or routing tables); (4) measure validator accept/reject decisions and execution-grounded correctness by executing accepted configs in the simulator; (5) repeat with randomized seeds to produce per-condition distributions. Preregistration will fix task set, perturbation magnitudes, sample size, and retry policy.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task, per-condition records including: LLM-generated config text, validator decision (accept/reject), simulated execution result (reachability matrix, ACL violation indicators, loop detection), perturbation parameters, timestamps, and hashes; aggregated counts and rates for false-acceptance, false-rejection, true-acceptance, and accepted-correct fraction across mismatch levels.
candidates.primary_outcome: Change in validator unsafe-acceptance rate (proportion of accepted configs that are execution-incorrect) as a function of state-mismatch magnitude; operational threshold where validator utility (accepted-correct fraction) no longer exceeds the no-validator baseline.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute per-condition proportions (unsafe-acceptance, false-rejection) with 95% binomial CIs; use logistic regression to model unsafe-acceptance as a function of mismatch magnitude and task type; compare matched vs each mismatch level with paired difference-in-proportions tests (McNemar or bootstrap paired tests depending on pairing); report effect sizes and model-predicted mismatch threshold where validator benefit crosses zero; perform failure-mode taxonomic analysis of accepted incorrect configs.
risks: Simulator/oracle may not fully capture vendor-specific semantics, limiting external validity.
LLM outputs may require normalization/parsing that introduces pre-evaluation bias.
Creating realistic state-mismatch scenarios may inadvertently produce infeasible conditions (handled via preregistered sanity checks).
Overfitting validator heuristics to the chosen synthetic topologies.

candidates.title: Evaluating Prompt-Injection and Retrieval/Tool-Channel Attacks on Agentic NetOps Pipelines and Layered Defenses
candidates.research_question: What is the empirical effectiveness of adversarial indirect/prompt-injection attacks delivered via retrieval and tool outputs against an agentic NetOps pipeline, and how much do layered defenses (RAG grounding, deterministic validators, and tool sandboxing) reduce successful attack rates?
hypotheses: An unguarded agentic pipeline with retrieval and tool integration will exhibit a non-negligible adversarial success rate (successful unsafe config application) when the retrieval/tool corpus contains crafted injection payloads.

A defense-in-depth configuration combining retrieval sanitization (trusted-source filtering), RAG grounding with provenance, and a deterministic validator will reduce successful adversarial injections by ≥70% relative to the unguarded baseline.
candidates.proposed_design: Construct an agentic NetOps pipeline prototype using public components: (1) retrieval index seeded with benign doc corpus plus injected adversarial documents simulating compromised knowledge sources and tool outputs; (2) tool-integration layer that returns attacker-crafted CLI snippets when queried by the agent (simulated tool); (3) LLM-based plan/config generator invoked with identical prompts across experiments; (4) defense configurations: none, RAG-only, validator-only, RAG+validator+sandbox; (5) define attack success as an accepted config that, when executed in simulator, performs an unsafe action (ACL breach, route hijack, blackhole); (6) run a battery of adversarial payloads (obfuscation, indirect instruction, instruction-masking) across tasks and defenses; (7) measure attack success rates and provenance/trust metrics. Preregister attack corpus, defenses, and success criteria.
candidates.expected_data: Per-run logs with pipeline inputs, retrieval hits and provenance, tool outputs, LLM responses, defense actions (sanitization, rejects), simulator execution outcomes, and binary attack-success labels; aggregated success rates per defense, per-attack-type and per-task.
candidates.primary_outcome: Relative reduction in adversarial attack success rate for the combined defense compared to the unguarded baseline, with statistical significance and confidence intervals.
candidates.analysis_outline: Estimate attack success proportions with 95% CIs per defense; compare defenses with pairwise proportion tests (McNemar or bootstrap) and compute relative risk reductions; stratify by attack type and task; analyze false-blocking rates (benign configs blocked) and compute trade-offs (precision/recall for blocking); present exemplar successful/instrumented failure cases for qualitative analysis.
risks: Constructing realistic adversarial payloads may require domain expertise and could accidentally replicate real vulnerabilities (experiments limited to simulated environments and public corpora).
Defense tuning to the known attack corpus may overestimate real-world robustness.
Tool-sandbox simulation may not capture all live tool integration subtleties, affecting external validity.

candidates.title: An Execution-Grounded Benchmark for LLM-Generated Network Configurations: Metrics, Oracles, and Adversarial Tests
candidates.research_question: Can an execution-grounded benchmark that combines executable oracles (reachability, ACL compliance, loop/blackhole detection) with adversarial injections produce reproducible metrics that diverge from language-level correctness measures and better reflect operational safety?
hypotheses: Language-level similarity metrics and LM intrinsic scores (e.g., token-likelihood, BLEU-like measures) will correlate weakly (Pearson r < 0.5) with execution-grounded correctness (reachability/ACL success) across a diverse task set.

Inclusion of adversarial test cases in the benchmark will reveal systematic failure modes not apparent in language-only evaluations and will change relative model rankings compared to language-only metrics.
candidates.proposed_design: Design and release a public benchmark corpus derived from permissively licensed config fragments and synthesized topologies: (1) define tasks (intent-to-config for reachability, ACL modification, and routing policy); (2) implement executable oracles using a network simulator to assess correctness; (3) include adversarially perturbed tasks (maliciously ambiguous intents, corrupted repository entries); (4) run multiple LLM prompting strategies to produce candidate configs; (5) evaluate each candidate with both language-level metrics and execution-level oracles; (6) compute metric correlations and rank stability under adversarial additions. Publish dataset, evaluation code, and scoring scripts for reproducibility.
candidates.expected_data: Benchmark dataset (tasks, reference configs, adversarial cases), per-model per-task outputs, language-level metric scores, execution-oracle binary/continuous correctness measures, correlation matrices, model ranking lists under varied metric sets, and artifact hashes.
candidates.primary_outcome: Empirical correlation between language-level metrics and execution-grounded correctness (expectation: low correlation) and demonstration that adversarial cases alter model rankings and reveal operationally-relevant failures.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute pairwise Pearson and Spearman correlations between each language metric and each execution metric with bootstrap CIs; perform rank-correlation tests to compare ranking stability with and without adversarial cases; use cluster analysis to identify failure-mode groups; report example failure cases and per-task metric breakdowns; provide reproducibility checklist and artifact hashes.
risks: Public corpora may lack vendor-specific diversity, limiting representativeness.
Simulated oracles may not capture all production execution nuances, risking overconfidence.
Benchmark design choices (task difficulty, adversary selection) could bias evaluation toward certain defenses.

candidates.title: Iteration Dynamics and Optimal Stopping for Generate–Verify–Repair Loops in LLM-Assisted NetOps
candidates.research_question: What are the per-iteration improvement dynamics of a bounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop for intent-to-configuration tasks, and can an empirically derived stopping rule achieve near-maximum correctness while reducing model-call costs?
hypotheses: For typical NetOps IaC tasks, marginal correctness improvement in a GVR loop will exhibit diminishing returns and plateau by the 2nd–4th iteration for most tasks.

A simple stopping rule based on validator-stability (no validator-accepted improvement in two consecutive iterations) will retain ≥95% of the maximum attainable correctness while reducing total model calls by ≥30%.
candidates.proposed_design: Preregistered iterative experiment: (1) select representative intent-to-config tasks; (2) run a GVR pipeline where each iteration uses the LLM to propose fixes guided by deterministic validator feedback; (3) cap iterations at a conservative maximum (e.g., 6); (4) record per-iteration correctness, validator decisions, and model-call counts; (5) evaluate multiple stopping rules (fixed k, validator-stability, marginal-improvement threshold) against full-run correctness and cost; (6) analyze iteration-to-plateau distribution and compute cost-benefit trade-offs.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task iteration logs: candidate configs per iteration, validator outputs, execution-grounded correctness per iteration, model-call counts, and timestamps; aggregated per-task iteration curves and stopping-rule performance metrics (correctness retained vs calls saved).
candidates.primary_outcome: Distribution of plateau iteration numbers across tasks and empirical performance of stopping rules (correctness retained and percentage model-call reduction), identifying a recommended stopping heuristic.
candidates.analysis_outline: Plot per-task and aggregated iteration improvement curves; compute median and IQR of plateau iteration; compare stopping rules via paired analyses of retained correctness and model-call savings; use nonparametric tests for differences in retained correctness; present failure-case analyses where iterations fail to converge.
risks: Stopping heuristics tuned on the selected task set may not generalize to other NetOps tasks.
Validator brittleness may produce false stability signals, causing premature stopping.
Synthetic tasks may underrepresent complex real-world iterative repair needs.
